title: Dedicated pool sizing and SLA decision framework for guaranteed throughput vs flexible autoscaling
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Summary:
We need a repeatable decision framework for sizing Dedicated GPU pools and converting enterprise customer intake requirements (SLA latency/availability, reserved throughput, burst allowance) into explicit allocation and autoscaling policies. Current intake conversations are inconsistent: some customers ask for 'guaranteed throughput', others ask for '99th percentile latency SLAs', and our sales/solutions engineers translate these to ad-hoc GPU counts or conservative buffers. This ticket scopes a product-side rubric and a small pilot to validate assumptions with telemetry and cost estimates.

Goals:
- Produce a clear rubric that maps customer asks to: reserved throughput (qPS), baseline GPU class (e.g., H100/A100/L40s equivalence), headroom multiplier, and burst credit policy.
- Define a recommended autoscaling policy that balances strict reserved guarantees vs. flexible elastic capacity (soft-SLOs + fallback routing).
- Provide engineering with a compact payload (algorithm + example configs) they can use in the intake UI and the capacity provisioning microservice.

Scope / Non-goals:
- IN-SCOPE: Product decision matrix, acceptance criteria for pilot, telemetry events to track, intake UI copy suggestions, one pilot with a single enterprise customer (Finova), baseline cost estimation method.
- OUT-OF-SCOPE: Implementation-level autoscaler code changes, billing migration, multi-tenant isolation architecture.

Proposed decision matrix (high level):
1) Intake inputs: target qPS (requests/sec), average tokens/request, p99 latency target, acceptable tail-loss (fraction of requests allowed to use fallback), preferred GPU family constraint.
2) Compute baseline GPU allocation: baseline_gpus = ceil((qPS * avg_tokens * concurrency_factor) / tokens_per_gpu_sec) where concurrency_factor defaults to 1.2 for production safety.
3) Headroom policy: headroom_multiplier = 1.25 for enterprise SLAs, 1.1 for non-critical workloads. Apply to baseline_gpus for reserved pool.
4) Burst credits: allocate transient burst credits equivalent to up to 30% additional qPS for 5 minute windows; expire and refill per rolling window.
5) Autoscaling policy: prefer capacity reservations + soft autoscaling above reserved baseline. Soft autoscaling can lease spot/burst capacity with best-effort latency and explicit routing of overflow to fallback model variants.
6) GPU class selection heuristics: map expected sequence length and model family to GPU family with a preference order (H100 > A100 > L40s) but allow customer-specified constraints. Include a 'compatibility score' that penalizes cross-architecture quantization needed.

Tradeoffs and rationale:
- Conservative reserved allocations reduce runtime outage risk but increase cost. We propose headroom multipliers instead of large rounded-up GPU counts to avoid overspend while still meeting most enterprise SLAs.
- Burst credit model reduces cold-provision costs for infrequent spikes but requires a clear customer-visible contract (how often and how big a burst).
- Soft autoscaling (best-effort GPUs or cross-region spill) handles unexpected spikes but must be surfaced in the SLA as potentially higher latency.

Acceptance criteria (for PM):
- Deliver a one-page rubric + worked examples for three archetypes: low-throughput/high-latency-strict (e.g., fraud scoring), high-throughput/loose-latency (e.g., embeddings ingestion), hybrid chat workloads.
- Draft intake form fields and default values for headroom and burst policy to be embedded in the sales intake UI.
- Agreement from Eng on an implementable telemetry plan with 6 required events and dashboards.
- Pilot kickoff with Finova scheduled and scope agreed (2-week data collection, 1-week configuration validation).

Telemetry & dashboards (minimum events):
- reserved_pool_requested_qps
- reserved_pool_allocated_gpus
- reserved_pool_headroom_multiplier
- reserved_pool_burst_consumed_tokens
- sla_breach_count_reason (e.g., capacity, network, model-failure)
- fallback_routed_requests_percent

Pilot plan with Finova (example):
1) Week 0: kick-off + real traffic sample (1 day) to measure avg tokens & tail.
2) Week 1: provision reserved baseline per rubric with headroom multiplier 1.25, enable burst credits (30% for 5m windows).
3) Week 2: run with monitoring; collect telemetry and cost metrics; engineering to validate autoscale triggers in sandbox.
4) Week 3: review and decide final production settings and contract language.

Docs / links:
- Intake draft doc (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/DED/Reserved+Throughput+Allocator+Draft
- Example PR for capacity config prototype (GitHub): https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/8742
- Finova pilot brief (Drive): https://drive.google.com/finova-pilot-brief

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Default concurrency_factor: 1.2 or 1.5? (Engineering leaning to 1.5 for multi-tenant headroom).
- How to bill for burst credits: included vs metered? Finance input required.
- Should we support explicit GPU family locking in the intake (yes for regulated customers) or only suggest preference (preferred by default)?

Next steps / owners:
- PM (Maya) to iterate rubric and produce final one-pager (due 2026-03-25).
- Eng (Alex/Oliver) to confirm tokens_per_gpu_sec estimates for primary model families and sign off on concurrency_factor by 2026-03-12.
- Solutions Eng to line up Finova pilot and share sample traffic by 2026-03-05.
